title: NCC Study Documentation
text:
Welcome
This is the documentation site for the Norwegian COVID-19 Cohort (NCC / Koronastudien). It collects the study manual and best-practice guides used by study personnel and research collaborators.
The site is organised into two parts:

title: NCC Study Documentation
text:
How to use this site
Use the sidebar to navigate, or the search box (top of the sidebar) to jump to a topic. Each page has an “Edit this page” link once the repository URL is configured, so corrections can be proposed directly.

title: NCC Study Documentation
text:
Contributing
This documentation is maintained collaboratively by the NCC study group. To propose a change, edit the relevant .qmd file and open a pull request — see README.md in the repository for the full workflow.






Important



This site is intended for documentation only. It must never contain participant-level data, personal identifiers, or restricted registry material. Assume everything here is publicly visible.


Last built: August 4, 2026

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.1 Overview
The NCC-study (Koronastudien) combines self-reported questionnaire data with linked national health-registry data and biological samples. This page describes each of those sources, how participants consent, and how the data reaches the secure processing environment. For how the resulting datasets are structured and joined, see Data management.
Data is collected through three channels that are later linked on a single participant key:
All three are delivered into TSD (Tjenester for Sensitive Data), where they are processed into research-ready datasets. Person-level data never leaves TSD.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
Questionnaires — participants answer online questionnaires hosted on Nettskjema, the University of Oslo’s survey platform.
Health registries — national health registries contribute records for consenting participants under the study’s approvals.
Biological samples — biobank and laboratory results (e.g. serology from dried blood spots).








Tip



Every source is ultimately keyed to deltaker_id, the study’s unique participant identifier, which is what makes the sources joinable. How that key is assigned is covered under Participant identification.

title: 2  Data collection
text:

NoteTODO — questionnaire schedule



Describe when each questionnaire was fielded and the intended follow-up cadence (e.g. baseline at enrolment, follow-ups at fixed intervals). Note which questionnaires are closed (no longer accepting responses) versus still open.



2.2.1 How questionnaire data is collected

Participants complete questionnaires online in Nettskjema.
Each submission is a single response; a participant answers a given questionnaire at most once, which is why the delivered data is naturally wide (one row per participant per form).
Nettskjema assigns each submission an internal reference (submission_reference). This is used during processing to identify the participant, but is not stable across re-exports and is not a research variable.
The questionnaire item text and response options are the authoritative definition of each variable; they are preserved as variable and value labels in the delivered data.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.3 Consent
Consent is handled as a separate datastream from the questionnaires, so that participation status can be managed independently of the substantive responses.

Consent capture — participants provide informed consent, recorded via Nettskjema.
Identification lookups — consent processing maintains lookup tables that map a participant’s Nettskjema submission_reference, phone number, or email to their deltaker_id.
Revocation — participants may withdraw at any time. Withdrawn participants are recorded on a revoked-consent list, and their responses are removed during processing.







Important



Consent is not a one-time gate. Revoked consents are re-applied on every processing run, so a withdrawal removes the participant from all subsequently delivered datasets. Analyses are always run against the current consent state.

Summarise what participants consent to (questionnaires, registry linkage, biobank use), the legal basis / approvals (REK, data protection), and how withdrawal is requested.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.4 From Nettskjema to TSD
Questionnaire and consent data move from Nettskjema into the secure environment automatically:

Participants submit responses in Nettskjema.
The TSD data loader transfers submissions into TSD as raw, semicolon-delimited CSV files (one file per questionnaire form).
Inside TSD, each raw file is processed independently into a cleaned, labelled per-form dataset.

Because TSD has no network access, everything downstream of this transfer — cleaning, linkage, analysis — happens entirely within TSD. No study data is stored or processed outside it.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.5 Health registry linkage
For consenting participants, national health registries contribute records that extend the self-reported data with objective, longitudinal health information. Registry data is delivered to TSD as approved extracts and linked to participants on the study key.








Registry
Full name
Contributes




MSIS
Meldingssystem for smittsomme sykdommer
Notifiable infectious-disease diagnoses (incl. SARS-CoV-2)


SYSVAK
Nasjonalt vaksinasjonsregister
Vaccinations (incl. COVID-19 doses)


DÅR
Dødsårsaksregisteret
Cause-of-death records


NPR
Norsk pasientregister
Hospital / specialist-care contacts


LMR
Legemiddelregisteret
Dispensed prescription medications









Note



Registry data is often longitudinal (multiple events per participant over time). Before delivery it is summarised to one row per participant so it stays joinable on deltaker_id without inflating row counts. What each registry extract covers (time span, event types) is fixed by the approved data delivery.








Important



Some registry deliveries carry strict handling conditions — for example, a national identity number may be prohibited from being stored alongside the registry records, with linkage performed through a project-specific key only. These conditions are enforced in processing and are why registry data lives in the most restricted storage tier.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.6 Biological samples
The study also collects biological material and derived laboratory results.

Dried blood spots (DBS) and related samples are collected from participants.
Laboratory analyses (e.g. serology / antibody measurements) are performed and the results delivered to TSD.
Biobank results are linked to participants on deltaker_id and processed the same way as other sources.







NoteTODO — biobank details



Describe how and when biological samples were collected, which assays were run, and how results are reported back into the study.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.7 Participant identification
Every source above is linked to a single key, deltaker_id, which is what allows questionnaires, registries, and biobank data to be joined together.
During processing, deltaker_id is assigned by matching each response against the consent lookup tables, in order of reliability:

Nettskjema submission_reference
Phone number
Email address

Once assigned, deltaker_id is the only identifier retained for linkage; direct contact details (phone, email) are dropped from processed data. See Data management for how deltaker_id is used to join datasets.

title: 3  Data management
text:
3.1 The shape of the data
This page describes the conventions you need to know to work with NCC-study (Koronastudien) data: how datasets are structured, what the different delivery formats are, how sensitive data is separated, and how to join data sources correctly. It is aimed at researchers and analysts using the delivered data — not at the people maintaining the processing pipeline.
Every delivered dataset — whether a single questionnaire file, a topic-specific dataset, or the full legacy dataset — follows the same three rules. Together these make any two files safe to join.

title: 3  Data management
text:
deltaker_id is the join key. It is the unique participant identifier and appears as the first column of every file. It is the only key you ever join on.
One row per participant. Delivered datasets are in wide format: one row per deltaker_id, no duplicates. Longitudinal registry data is pre-summarised to wide before delivery, so it never causes fan-out.
Variable names are globally unique. Every variable is prefixed with its form, so columns from different files never collide when joined.







Tip



Because of rules 1–3, joining is always a clean 1:1 merge on deltaker_id. If a join produces more rows than participants, something is wrong — stop and check before analysing.



3.1.1 Variable prefixes
Each questionnaire item is prefixed with the form it came from. Derived and computed variables have their own prefixes.

title: 3  Data management
text:
3.2 Labelled data
Delivered files are labelled: variables carry a human-readable variable label and, for categorical items, value labels. Both Norwegian and English labels are maintained. In R these arrive as haven_labelled vectors.






Note



Treat labels as documentation, not as data. Convert to explicit factors when you need the text (e.g. haven::as_factor()), and keep the underlying codes for modelling. Never hard-code a label string as a filter condition — value codes are stable across releases, label wording may be refined.


Question text and value labels are the semantic definition of an item and are stable even when the underlying variable name changes between pipeline versions. If you are ever unsure what a variable means, the label — not the name — is the source of truth. A codebook (variable names, labels, value labels, types) is delivered alongside every dataset.

title: 3  Data management
text:
3.3 Which dataset should I use?
Two delivery modes are produced from the same underlying per-form files, so they are always mutually consistent.

Topic datasets (recommended for new work)Legacy full dataset


Curated, pre-assembled datasets scoped to a research area — e.g. CLOC, long COVID, vaccine. Each contains only the forms, registry data, and derived variables relevant to that topic. They are smaller, faster to load, and easier to reason about. Start here for any new project.
cloc_dataset.qs
long_covid_dataset.qs
vaccine_dataset.qs


A single wide dataset joining all forms with all derived variables, mirroring the historical full_deriv.qs. Variable names, prefixes, and derived variables match the old pipeline, so existing analysis scripts keep working unchanged. It is large and memory-hungry — use it only when you specifically need backward compatibility with an established pipeline.
full_deriv.qs









TipRule of thumb



New project → topic dataset. Maintaining an old pipeline that already loads full_deriv.qs → keep using the legacy dataset until you have time to migrate. Both are built from the same source data, so results agree.

title: 3  Data management
section: 3.4 Data sensitivity: research vs admin tiers
text:
3.4 Data sensitivity: research vs admin tiers
Data is separated into two tiers by sensitivity. As a researcher you work in the research (yellow) tier.








Tier
Access
Contains




Research (yellow)
Researchers + admins
Delivered per-form files, topic and legacy datasets, codebooks. Free-text / elaboration fields are suppressed.


Admin (black/red)
Data managers only
Full files including free-text elaboration fields and raw consent data.



Free-text and open-ended “elaboration” fields (typically named *_elaborate), and any field that could re-identify a participant, are classified as sensitive and are not present in the research-tier files.

3.4.1 Requesting sensitive fields
If your analysis genuinely needs a suppressed field — for example free-text responses for a qualitative analysis — the data manager can assemble a custom dataset that includes only the specific sensitive columns you need, alongside your standard research variables. This custom dataset is shared with you individually and does not enter the general research area.






Note



Every release of admin-tier data is an explicit, logged action by the data manager — it is not something you can trigger yourself. Request it early if you anticipate needing it.

title: 3  Data management
text:
3.5 Joining datasets
All joins are 1:1 on deltaker_id. Pick the join type by which participants you want to keep.








Goal
Join
Result




Everyone from both files
full join
Keeps all participants; NA for forms not completed


Only those who completed both
inner join
Smaller; no cross-form missingness


Start from one file, enrich it
left join
Keeps all rows of the left file



For most cohort analyses, full join is the safe default: it preserves the whole cohort and represents non-participation as missing rather than silently dropping people.

RStataSPSS


library(dplyr)
library(qs)          # or qs2 for newer files

b1 <- qread("B1.qs")
f1 <- qread("F1.qs")
f2 <- qread("F2.qs")

# Full join — keep the whole cohort
df <- b1 |>
  full_join(f1, by = "deltaker_id") |>
  full_join(f2, by = "deltaker_id")

# Sanity check: no join should increase the participant count
stopifnot(nrow(df) == n_distinct(df$deltaker_id))


use "B1.dta", clear

merge 1:1 deltaker_id using "F1.dta", nogenerate
merge 1:1 deltaker_id using "F2.dta", nogenerate

* _merge == 1  only in base (did not complete the other form)
* _merge == 2  only in using file
* _merge == 3  in both


* Sort every file by the key before matching.
GET FILE='B1.sav'.
SORT CASES BY deltaker_id.
SAVE OUTFILE='B1_sorted.sav'.

GET FILE='F1.sav'.
SORT CASES BY deltaker_id.
SAVE OUTFILE='F1_sorted.sav'.

MATCH FILES
  /FILE='B1_sorted.sav'
  /FILE='F1_sorted.sav'
  /BY deltaker_id.
EXECUTE.









Warning



Always verify the row count after joining. A 1:1 merge on deltaker_id should never produce more rows than there are participants. If it does, you have likely picked up a file that is not deduplicated — do not proceed.

title: 3  Data management
text:
3.6 Good practice checklist

Start from a topic dataset unless you specifically need legacy compatibility.
Join only on deltaker_id, and check the row count afterwards.
Read variable meanings from the label / codebook, not the name.
Filter on value codes, not label text.
Request any sensitive fields from the data manager early.
Keep all person-level data inside TSD — export results only.
